wiki_excerpt:
Nelumbo nucifera, also known as Padma (Sanskrit: पद्म, romanized: Padma, lit. 'Lotus') or Kamala (Sanskrit: कमल, lit. 'Lotus'), sacred lotus, pink lotus, Indian lotus, or simply lotus, is one of two extant species of aquatic plant in the family Nelumbonaceae. It is sometimes colloquially called water lily, though this more often refers to members of the family Nymphaeaceae. The lotus belongs in the order Proteales.


Description
Lotus plants are adapted to grow in the flood plains of slow-moving rivers and delta areas. Stands of lotus drop hundreds of thousands of seeds every year to the bottom of the pond. 
Some sprout immediately, though most are eaten by wildlife. The remaining seeds can remain dormant for an extensive period of time as the pond silt fills in and dries out. During flood conditions, sediments containing these seeds are broken open, and the dormant seeds rehydrate and begin a new lotus colony.
Lotus plants are cultivated in nutrient-rich, loamy, and often flooded soils, requiring warm temperatures and specific planting depths, with propagation via rhizomes, seeds, or tissue culture. It is harvested by hand or machine for stolons, flowers, seeds, and rhizomes over several months depending on climate and variety.
It is the national flower of India and unofficially of Vietnam. It has large leaves and flowers that can regulate their temperature, produces long-living seeds, and contains bioactive alkaloids. Under favourable circumstances, the seeds of this aquatic perennial may remain viable for many years, with the oldest recorded lotus germination being from seeds 1,300 years old recovered from a dry lakebed in northeastern China. Therefore, the Chinese regard the plant as a symbol of longevity.
It has a very wide native distribution, ranging from East Asia (north to the Amur region) through northern Indochina and central and northern India (at altitudes up to 1,400 m (4,600 ft) in the southern Himalayas),; the Russian populations have sometimes been referred to as Nelumbo komarovii, with isolated locations at the Caspian Sea. Today, the species also occurs in southern India, Sri Lanka, virtually all of Southeast Asia, New Guinea, and northern and eastern Australia, but this is probably the result of human translocations. It has a very long history (c. 3,000 years) of being cultivated for its edible seeds and is commonly cultivated in water gardens. It is a highly symbolic and versatile plant used in religious offerings (especially in Hinduism and Buddhism) and diverse culinary traditions across Asia, with its flowers, seeds, and rhizomes valued for spiritual, cultural, and nutritional purposes. It holds deep cultural, spiritual, and religious significance across Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Ismailism, and Chinese culture, symbolizing purity, enlightenment, spiritual awakening, and divine beauty, and is widely depicted in art, architecture, and literature.

grok_lead: Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn., commonly known as the sacred lotus or Indian lotus, is a perennial aquatic herb in the family Nelumbonaceae, distinguished by its large, peltate leaves floating on water surfaces and solitary, showy flowers rising above on long peduncles, with rhizomes embedded in muddy substrates. Native to tropical and subtropical regions of Asia âfrom Iran to Japan and southeastern Asia âand northern Australia, it has been widely introduced elsewhere, including North America, where it inhabits shallow freshwater bodies such as ponds, lakes, slow-moving rivers, and wetlands typically 0.3 to 1.0 meters deep. The plant's ecology involves adaptation to stagnant or slow-moving waters, where rhizomes facilitate vegetative spread and seed banks enable long-term persistence, with viable seeds documented to germinate after centuries of dormancy. Flowers exhibit thermoregulation to attract pollinators, and leaves display self-cleaning properties due to their micro- and nanostructures, though empirical studies emphasize the role of epicuticular waxes in hydrophobicity. Various partsârhizomes, seeds, leaves, and flowersâare utilized in traditional cuisines and medicines across Asia; for instance, lotus seeds provide nutritional value with bioactive compounds supporting antioxidant and hepatoprotective effects, while embryos address nervous disorders in traditional Chinese formulations. Culturally, N. nucifera holds profound symbolism in Hinduism and Buddhism as emblematic of purity and enlightenment, arising pristine from mud, and serves as the national flower of India and Vietnam, influencing art, rituals, and even political iconography such as party symbols. Pharmacological research validates diverse bioactivities, including anti-inflammatory and antidiabetic properties from phytochemicals like alkaloids and flavonoids, though clinical evidence remains preliminary and derived largely from in vitro and animal models. In non-native regions, it can form dense stands altering aquatic ecosystems, prompting management as a potential invasive species.
